books.section: Topic 8.10 The African-American Civil Rights Movement (1960s)
The Civil Rights Movement in the 1960s: From Integration to Black Power

source: original; stimulus is an original account drawn from the grounding books

stimulus.source_note: Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.10, "The Freedom Rides (1961)"; 5 Steps Ch. 27; Princeton Ch. 12). The Boynton date, the Anniston firebombing, and the November 1, 1961 effective date are verified against the Encyclopedia of Alabama and Britannica summaries of the ICC order (September 22, 1961).
stimulus.text: In December 1960 the Supreme Court ruled in Boynton v. Virginia that segregation in bus terminals serving interstate travel was unconstitutional. Southern states kept enforcing their own segregation rules anyway. In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality (CORE) sent Black and white riders together on buses through the South to test whether the ruling was being enforced. Near Anniston, Alabama, a white mob slashed a bus's tires and then firebombed the bus. Television carried pictures of the burning bus and beaten riders across the country. President Kennedy sent federal marshals to protect the riders, and Attorney General Robert Kennedy asked the Interstate Commerce Commission to ban segregation in interstate travel. In September 1961 the commission ordered segregation ended in interstate bus terminals, effective November 1, 1961.

stem: The attack on the bus near Anniston best shows which of the following?

options.text: Southern states had already accepted the Boynton ruling before the rides began
options.misconception: The passage says Southern states kept enforcing segregation, the opposite of accepting the ruling.

options.text: The Freedom Riders were welcomed by local police in Alabama
options.misconception: A mob firebombed the bus; nothing in the passage shows police welcoming the riders.

options.text: Television cameras caused the violence by arriving before the riders did
options.misconception: The cameras carried pictures of the violence; they did not cause the mob's attack.

options.text: White resistance to desegregation could turn violent when federal law was challenged

rationales.A: The states kept enforcing their own segregation rules, so they had not accepted the ruling.
rationales.B: The riders were attacked by a mob, not welcomed by police.
rationales.C: Television reported the attack; the mob slashed the tires and firebombed the bus.
rationales.D: The passage shows a mob using fire to stop riders who were testing a federal court ruling.
rationales.general:
1. The riders were testing a Supreme Court ruling on interstate travel.
2. Near Anniston a mob slashed the bus tires and firebombed the bus.
3. That violence answered a legal challenge with force.
4. The attack shows how violent white resistance could be when federal law was tested.
Remember: Violence against a legal test shows the law alone had not changed behavior.
